claims.text: Corrosion resistance in steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is governed by engineered microstructural features that accelerate and stabilize passive-film formation.
Controlled heat treatments of Mo/Ni-alloyed carbon steels induce coherent Mo/Ni-rich precipitates.
The induced Mo/Ni-rich precipitates act as preferential nucleation sites for passive oxide films.
Controlled oxidation of high-chromium low-alloy steel enhances chromium diffusion to the surface.
Surface-directed chromium diffusion produces a self-healing Cr2O3 film that impedes corrosion.
The carbon-steel baseline has a homogeneous microstructure without significant precipitates.
The high-chromium-steel baseline has an undeveloped passive film and an unmodified chromium distribution.
Coherent Mo/Ni-rich precipitates can occur at grain boundaries or within grains.
Mo/Ni-rich precipitates lower the activation barrier for oxide-film nucleation.
Lowering the oxide-nucleation barrier produces rapid and spatially uniform passive-film formation.
Rapid and uniform passive-film formation mitigates localized corrosion in the carbon steel.
A self-healing Cr2O3 film repairs defects and inhibits ion transfer.
Inhibiting ion transfer through the Cr2O3 film reduces corrosion of the high-chromium steel.
Heat-treated carbon-steel samples will form more uniform and adherent passive films than untreated controls.
Heat-treated carbon-steel samples will exhibit less localized corrosion than untreated controls.
Oxidation-treated high-chromium-steel samples will exhibit lower corrosion current densities than baseline specimens.
Oxidation-treated high-chromium-steel samples will exhibit longer passivation times than baseline specimens.
Oxidation-treated high-chromium-steel samples will exhibit greater surface chromium enrichment than baseline specimens.
The carbon-steel mechanism is proposed to hold for Mo/Ni-alloyed carbon steel in high-chloride media at approximately 70 degrees Celsius.
The high-chromium-steel mechanism is proposed to hold in neutral to mildly alkaline aqueous environments at 90–120 degrees Celsius.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism predict accelerated or rapid passive-film formation, whereas the predicted outcome specifies longer passivation times. If 'passivation time' means time required to reach passivity, these predictions conflict; the intended meaning may instead have been longer persistence of passivity.
